newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe, Rwanda accuse world tribunal.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe, Rwanda accuse world tribunal.

text.p: Zimbabwe and Rwanda on Thursday accused the United Nations of racial bias, saying it was moving faster to bring Bosnian war criminals to justice but was foot- dragging in bringing to book perpetrators of Rwanda's genocide.

Saying they were unhappy with the slow progress of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), Zimbabwean Defence Minister Moven Mahachi and Rwandan Vice-President Paul Kagame urged the international community to help push its work forward.

"What the international tribunal has done is very unfair. They are concentrating on Bosnia instead of Rwanda's problems. Some of us think that's a biased approach, biased in that the Bosnians are white and the Rwandese, who are black, are neglected," Mahachi told reporters.

"They (the U.N.) should have put a lot of effort to sort out the problems of Rwanda. They are now concentrating on their kith and kin in Bosnia," he said at a press conference held at the end of Kagame's three-day visit to Zimbabwe.
The tribunal was set up by the U.N. to try leaders of a wave of ethnic cleansing killings which claimed a million lives in the tiny central African country between April and July 1994.
Kagame, who is also Rwanda's defence minister, said the United Nations should give the ICTR more help to do its work faster.
Since its creation two years ago, the tribunal has managed to take only three suspects into custody. Its first trial was postponed on Wednesday to next March because Rutaganda is ill.

In Harare on Thursday, Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana, who was accompanying Kagame, said the U.N. had to work harder to bring to book those responsible for the 1994 genocide to help his country prevent future conflicts.

"I agree with the ministers (Mahachi and Kagame) that the U.N. is biased towards Bosnia (in trying war criminals). The U.N. failed to prevent the genocide in Rwanda in 1994. What they have to do now is to be successful in pushing and trying people who committed the genocide," he said.

Kagame was in Harare to ask Zimbabwe's help in training its army. His southern African trip also included South Africa where he requested Pretoria's aid in rebuilding Rwanda's justice system and its economy. Mahachi said Zimbabwe would respond positively to Kagame's request.
